payload.problem_addressed: Whether a neural Sudoku solver (LDT) that appears to deduce, branch, and revise is actually doing iterative search, versus being a one-shot predictor wrapped in an exact verifier.
payload.method_summary: Diagnostic analysis of LDT on clue-rich Sudoku: measures how much of the grid is committed in one forward pass, identifies 'first-pass poisoning' as the failure cause, ablates learned branching/MRV/backtracking/value-exclusion/shared-nogoods (CoLT) and constraint-graph attention vs positional tables, then tests two interventions -- digit-permutation training augmentation and test-time union over symmetry-transformed passes -- plus a from-scratch graph-coloring control.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper shows that a neural Sudoku solver marketed as performing branching search actually commits nearly the whole solution in a single forward pass and is functionally a one-shot predictor wrapped in an exact verifier; all failures trace to a single early, confident wrong deletion ('first-pass poisoning') rather than to search quality. It further shows that adding learned search machinery (CoLT) does not change which instances are solved, only how much wasted invalid-derivation compute is cut, and that two calibration/symmetry interventions -- digit-permutation augmentation and test-time union over symmetry-transformed passes -- dramatically raise accuracy without retraining. On an out-of-distribution graph-coloring task, the one-shot behavior disappears and search actually changes outcomes, delimiting where the diagnosis applies.
key_architecture_choices: CoLT: learned branching, MRV, backtracking, value exclusion, shared nogoods
metrics: Grid-cell commitment fraction after one forward pass
payload.headline_results: Digit-permutation augmentation raises 9x9 accuracy from below 1% to 96.5 +/- 0.3 across three seeds; test-time union over symmetry-transformed passes raises hard-slice checkpoints from 72.8-78.9% to 100% without retraining; CoLT cuts repeated invalid derivations 1,497-fold without changing which instances are solved.
claimed_advantages: Test-time symmetry-union intervention needs no retraining and reaches 100% on hard slices
Digit-permutation augmentation fixes near-zero accuracy with no architecture change
Diagnosis (first-pass poisoning) pinpoints exactly where/when failures are decided, not just that they occur
limitations: Diagnosis and interventions are specific to clue-rich completion; on from-scratch graph coloring the one-shot behavior disappears and search matters again
Constraint-graph attention only matches full-CoLT accuracy at a frozen training budget; positional tables need substantially longer training to catch up
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: The core diagnostic question -- is this verifier-screened autoregressive model actually doing search, or is it a one-shot predictor whose apparent best-of-N selection just amortizes a single confident (and sometimes wrong) forward pass? -- is directly analogous to hexgen's best-of-N-plus-frozen-verifier pipeline, and worth running as a sanity check (does hexgen's decoder 'first-pass poison' by locking in a wrong face/coordinate choice early, with the frozen verifier just filtering symptoms rather than the model doing real structural search?). Two concrete, low-cost transferable mechanisms: (1) test-time union over symmetry-transformed passes (run the encoder-decoder on several rotated/permuted views of the B-rep and union/vote the candidate programs before verifier screening) as a deployment-time robustness trick for the rotation/pose-robustness care area; (2) a permutation/relabeling-style data augmentation (analogous to digit-permutation here) over face/coordinate labels to break spurious ordering shortcuts, relevant to the domain-gap/tokenization-mismatch care area.
payload.reviewer_notes: Results are on toy combinatorial puzzles (Sudoku, graph coloring), not CAD/geometry, so the specific numbers don't transfer -- but the underlying methodology (probe how much of the output a single forward pass commits vs how much search actually contributes, then intervene with symmetry augmentation) is a cheap, generalizable diagnostic worth adapting to hexgen's own verifier-in-the-loop pipeline before investing further in search machinery. Only the abstract was available for this extraction (single-chunk paper text), so architectural and experimental details beyond the abstract are not grounded here.

payload.impact_rationale: If hexgen's verifier-screened decoder turns out to be 'first-pass poisoning' the same way LDT does, the diagnostic would explain otherwise-mysterious best-of-N failure modes, and the test-time symmetry-union trick showed a dramatic accuracy jump (72.8-78.9% to 100%) with no retraining in the analogous Sudoku setting -- but this is one data point from a very different (puzzle) domain, so the size of any real transfer to CAD/hex-meshing is uncertain.
payload.effort_rationale: Running the one-shot-vs-search diagnostic on existing rollouts is cheap instrumentation (S); building a production test-time symmetry-union pass (defining valid B-rep/program symmetries, running multiple transformed passes, and voting/unioning candidates before verifier screening) is a bounded but nontrivial engineering task, hence a moderate (not minimal) overall effort.
